description: How organisations profile target audiences and the marketing techniques used to reach them.
content_html:
Who Is the Product For?

Before a media organisation invests in production, it must decide who the product is intended to reach. A target audience is the specific group at whom a product is aimed. The target audience shapes every decision — the storylines chosen, the celebrities cast, the platforms used, the price charged. Without a clear target audience, marketing spending is wasted.

A target audience is often divided into a primary audience and a secondary audience. A magazine pitched at women aged 25–35 may also attract younger or older readers who share its interests — those are the secondary audience. Producers do not necessarily design for them, but they welcome them.

Mass and Niche Audiences

Media products can target either a mass audience or a niche audience. A mainstream national daily newspaper tries to reach the widest possible readership; a specialist cycling magazine is produced for a small group with a defined passion. The economics of the two are quite different: mass-audience products attract large advertising revenues; niche products often charge subscription premiums because they deliver advertisers a highly targeted, engaged readership that is harder to reach through mainstream channels.

Key Fact

Niche audiences are commercially valuable because they deliver advertisers a concentrated, highly engaged group. Advertisers often pay a premium for access to a defined niche rather than broadcasting to a mass audience where most members are not potential customers.

Assumptions Organisations Make About Audiences

Media producers rarely have direct contact with their audience. Instead they build an audience profile — a set of assumptions about who is likely to be watching, reading, listening or playing. These assumptions are built from research: surveys, focus groups, ratings data and increasingly from behavioural data collected online. Assumptions can also be shaped by stereotypes of certain demographic groups, which is one reason why audience profiles sometimes reinforce existing inequalities.

Genre conventions play a part here too. A horror film producer makes assumptions about who enjoys that genre based on prior audience data — and those assumptions then shape the marketing approach, the certificate sought from the classifier, and the platforms where the product is promoted.

The trailer is one of the oldest audience-targeting tools in media. A trailer condenses the appeal of a product into 60–180 seconds, targeting the assumed audience through music, cast, pace, and the moments selected. A teaser is shorter — often only 30 seconds — and deliberately withholds more information in order to build anticipation and conversation. A taster, more common in broadcasting, offers a brief clip or preview episode to give audiences a genuine sense of the content without fully revealing it.

Each type of promotional material makes choices about what to emphasise and what to conceal. A streaming-era teen drama might release a teaser that focuses on the emotional relationships between characters rather than the plot twist at the series’ end, because the target audience’s interest has been identified as character-driven. Those choices reflect assumptions about the audience.

Viral and Guerrilla Marketing

Viral marketing attempts to generate audience momentum without (or alongside) conventional paid advertising. The goal is for audiences to share, discuss and amplify the content themselves — making them unpaid distributors of the marketing message. An effective viral campaign exploits curiosity, humour, emotion or social identity to motivate sharing.

Guerrilla marketing uses surprise, spectacle or novelty to create shareable moments. A product might appear overnight on city hoardings without explanation, leaving audiences curious; an unusual public stunt or pop-up installation might generate news coverage and social media posts without any paid placement. The logic is that earned media — coverage and discussion that isn’t bought — carries more credibility than advertising because it appears organic.

Key Fact

Viral marketing relies on audiences sharing content voluntarily across digital platforms. Guerrilla marketing creates surprise encounters in unexpected physical or digital spaces to generate word-of-mouth and news coverage. Both aim to reach audiences without relying solely on paid advertising.

Social Media Activations and ARGs

Contemporary marketing campaigns extend across multiple platforms. Social media activations coordinate posts, countdowns, and interactive challenges across platforms to build anticipation and engage target audiences directly. An alternate reality game (ARG) goes further: clues are planted across websites, social platforms and physical spaces, inviting audiences to become investigators who unravel a story. ARGs work especially well for products targeting digitally engaged younger audiences who enjoy participatory, puzzle-based experiences.

Marketing professionals think in three categories. Paid media is advertising you buy: sponsored posts, television commercials, banner ads. Owned media is content you control directly: your official social media accounts, website, and branded YouTube channel. Earned media is coverage and discussion generated by others: a journalist writing about your campaign, a fan community speculating about your product, or viewers sharing your trailer. A modern marketing campaign tries to convert paid media investment into earned media reach, which carries credibility because it is not perceived as advertising.
exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to explain targeting or marketing techniques, name the specific technique, explain how it works, and then link it to the assumptions the producer is making about their target audience. The examiner wants to see that you understand the relationship between audience profiling and the marketing choices made — not just a description of what a trailer is.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Media organisations construct detailed audience profiles based on research and assumptions about their target audiences, which shape every production and marketing decision.
  • Trailers, teasers and tasters are traditional targeting tools; viral marketing, guerrilla marketing and social media activations are digital-era techniques that encourage audiences to become unpaid distributors of marketing messages.
  • The paid — owned — earned media framework explains how organisations try to convert advertising spend into organic reach and credibility.

practice_questions.text: Which of the following is an example of guerrilla marketing?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct answer is B. A) Incorrect — this is paid media advertising. B) Correct — an unannounced installation in a public space to generate surprise and conversation is guerrilla marketing. C) Incorrect — this is a traditional trailer. D) Incorrect — this is owned media.

practice_questions.text: Identify the term for the additional audience a media product may reach beyond its primary target group.
Identify what an 'audience profile' is and explain one reason why media organisations construct them.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: 1 mark for defining audience profile as a constructed set of assumptions about the typical target audience member. 1 mark for a developed reason — for example, to ensure every creative and marketing decision is directed at the most likely consumers, or to demonstrate to advertisers that the product reaches a specific, valuable group.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by 'viral marketing' and why media organisations use it.
practice_questions.marks: Developing: Gives a basic definition of viral marketing as something that spreads online. Secure: Accurately defines viral marketing as a strategy designed to encourage audiences to share content voluntarily and explains that it generates earned media reach without proportional advertising spend. Mastering: Precise definition plus a well-developed explanation of why this is commercially valuable (credibility of organic sharing, cost efficiency, audience-as-distributor logic), with a clear example context.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the use of a teaser campaign reflects the assumptions a media organisation makes about its target audience.
practice_questions.marks: Developing: Notes that teasers withhold information but does not connect this to audience assumptions. Secure: Explains that teaser campaigns are designed to generate curiosity and conversation, and that this reflects an assumption that the target audience is engaged enough to seek out further information and discuss the product socially. Mastering: Full explanation linking specific teaser design choices (withholding plot, focusing on tone) to detailed audience assumptions (the audience is digitally active, genre-literate, and values anticipation) and connecting to the concept of earned media.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a media organisation uses different marketing techniques to reach a target audience for a product you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Names one or two marketing techniques with limited connection to audience assumptions. Developing: Identifies two or three techniques with some explanation of how each targets the audience, but the analysis lacks depth; connections to audience profiling are superficial. Secure: Analyses at least three techniques with clear explanation of how each reflects assumptions about the target audience; uses appropriate terminology (primary audience, earned media, viral, niche/mass). Mastering: Sustained analytical argument comparing the effectiveness of different techniques, with precise reference to a named product's marketing strategy; explicitly links marketing choices to audience profile assumptions and connects to broader industry context (paid/owned/earned framework).

knowledge_checks.q: What term describes the main intended audience a media product is produced for?
Which type of media coverage is described as 'earned' media?
options: A television commercial bought by the producer
A sponsored post on social media
News coverage and fan discussion generated organically

knowledge_checks.q: A short promotional film that condenses the appeal of a media product into 60–180 seconds in order to attract an audience is called a _____.
An alternate reality game (ARG) works by planting clues across websites, social platforms and physical spaces to make audiences into _____ who unravel a story.
Match each marketing term to its definition.
right: A constructed set of assumptions about the typical target audience member
An unconventional approach creating surprise encounters in unexpected spaces
A strategy designed so audiences share content voluntarily

flashcard_questions.a: The specific group a media product is primarily designed to attract and address

flashcard_questions.q: How does a niche audience differ from a mass audience?
flashcard_questions.a: A niche audience is small and specialised; a mass audience is broad and large
A constructed set of assumptions about the typical target audience member's interests, habits and values

flashcard_questions.q: What makes earned media valuable to marketers?
flashcard_questions.a: It appears organic and credible because it is not perceived as paid advertising

flashcard_questions.q: What is viral marketing designed to do?
flashcard_questions.a: Encourage audiences to share content voluntarily so they become unpaid distributors

flashcard_questions.q: What distinguishes a teaser from a trailer?
flashcard_questions.a: A teaser is shorter and withholds more information to build anticipation

flashcard_questions.q: What is an alternate reality game (ARG)?
flashcard_questions.a: An interactive narrative spread across real-world and digital spaces, inviting audiences to solve clues
Unconventional marketing using surprise or spectacle in unexpected spaces to generate word-of-mouth

flashcard_questions.q: Name the three categories of media in the paid-owned-earned framework.
flashcard_questions.a: Paid (bought advertising), owned (producer-controlled channels), earned (organic coverage)

flashcard_questions.q: Why are niche audiences commercially valuable to advertisers?
flashcard_questions.a: They deliver a concentrated, highly engaged group that is hard to reach through mass channels

glossary_terms.definition: The specific group of people a media product is primarily designed to attract and address.
The main intended audience a product is produced for.
An additional audience a product may reach beyond its primary target.
A very large, broad audience that a media product tries to appeal to regardless of age, gender or background.
A small, specialised audience with a specific, shared interest or characteristic.
A constructed set of assumptions about the typical member of a target audience, including their interests, values, habits and spending power.
A short promotional film or broadcast that previews a media product to attract an audience.
A marketing strategy designed to encourage audiences to share content voluntarily, spreading awareness organically rather than through paid advertising.
An unconventional, low-cost marketing approach that creates surprising or interactive encounters with an audience in unexpected public or digital spaces.
An interactive networked narrative that uses the real world as a platform for storytelling, blurring the boundary between game and reality to engage a target audience.
